group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 58-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department in the late afternoon after three days of progressively worsening cough and left-sided chest discomfort that sharpened with deep inspiration and radiated toward the scapular tip. She reported low-grade chills but denied feeling overtly febrile, and she had remained fully oriented, continuing to manage household finances and converse normally with family up until the moment she chose to seek care. Her past medical history includes an embolic cerebrovascular accident six years earlier secondary to paroxysmal atrial flutter; she completed inpatient rehabilitation at that time and now manifests only a subtle pronator drift of the right arm when fatigued but no speech or gait disturbances. She also carries a long-standing diagnosis of chronic hepatitis C with bridging fibrosis documented on elastography two years ago, for which antiviral therapy was offered but deferred because of insurance issues; she has never developed ascites, encephalopathy, or variceal bleeding, and her most recent outpatient liver panel three months ago showed mild transaminitis but preserved synthetic function. She has no record of structural or ischemic cardiac dysfunction, has never been told she had reduced ejection fraction, and specifically denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or lower-extremity swelling at baseline. Her daily medications consist of apixaban for secondary stroke prevention, low-dose aspirin discontinued at the time anticoagulation was started, and intermittent acetaminophen for tension headaches. She quit smoking two decades ago after a 15-pack-year exposure and drinks one glass of wine with dinner perhaps twice a month; she has never used illicit substances. No recent antibiotic courses, hospital admissions, or invasive procedures are recorded, and she completed the current season’s influenza vaccination in early autumn. On arrival she was seated upright on the stretcher, speaking in full sentences, without labored respirations. Initial vital signs before any therapy revealed an oral temperature of 36.9 °C, pulse 87 beats per minute and regular, blood pressure 145/82 mm Hg in the left arm, respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute with symmetrical chest excursions, and oxygen saturation 91 % on ambient air that rose to 94 % when she was asked to perform sustained deep breaths for arterial sampling but before supplemental oxygen was applied. Her skin was warm and well perfused; mucous membranes were moist, and conjunctivae anicteric. Jugular venous contour was flat at 45 °, and there was no peripheral edema. Cardiac auscultation revealed a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Pulmonary examination uncovered decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the left posterior base with fine crackles just above that zone; no wheezing was appreciated. Abdomen was soft, nontender, and nondistended, with the liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin but without suggestion of fluid wave. Neurologic screening showed equal pupils, intact extraocular movements, fluent speech, and 5/5 strength throughout, replicating her known mild right-sided drift only after prolonged arms-outstretched testing; sensation and coordination were preserved, and gait was not assessed because of her chest discomfort. Finger-stick blood glucose measured 118 mg/dL. Venous blood was drawn and an arterial puncture performed prior to any intravenous fluids, antipyretics, or antibiotics. Laboratory results returned within the first hour demonstrated sodium 137 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 102 mEq/L, bicarbonate 26 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 31 mg/dL with paired creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, total bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL, AST 62 U/L, ALT 58 U/L, albumin 3.7 g/dL, and hematocrit 45 %. White blood cell count was 12.6 × 10⁹/L with 82 % neutrophils, platelets 210 × 10⁹/L, and INR 1.1 while on therapeutic anticoagulation. Arterial blood gas on room air revealed pH 7.44, PaCO₂ 37 mm Hg, PaO₂ 78 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 25 mEq/L. High-sensitivity troponin I was undetectable, and pro-BNP was within reference limits. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes, left ventricular hypertrophy, or conduction delay. A posterior-anterior and lateral portable chest radiograph obtained minutes later displayed a dense consolidation involving the left lower lobe accompanied by blunting of the left costophrenic angle and a meniscus sign consistent with a small pleural fluid collection; the cardiac silhouette was normal in size, mediastinum midline, and no diaphragmatic elevation or air-fluid level was evident on the contralateral side. No prior imaging was available for direct comparison, but bedside lung ultrasound performed by the emergency physician confirmed an anechoic stripe measuring approximately 1 cm in maximum thickness over the left hemidiaphragm with overlying hepatization of the lung parenchyma. Urinalysis, rapid respiratory viral panel, and two sets of blood cultures were sent but results were pending at the time of this note. Throughout the initial evaluation period she remained fully alert, answering questions cogently, and demonstrated stable hemodynamics without requirement for vasoactive support or supplemental oxygen beyond ambient air. The current assessment is a community-onset lung infection of the left lower lobe with associated parapneumonic effusion in a middle-aged woman whose history is notable for prior stroke with minimal residual deficit and chronic hepatitis C–related liver injury; laboratory and imaging data were obtained prior to any therapeutic intervention to allow accurate baseline characterization.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
- Demographics: for a woman, start with age minus 10: 58 − 10 = 48. No nursing-home residence documented → 0 additional points.
- Comorbidities: chronic hepatitis C with bridging fibrosis qualifies as liver disease → 20; prior embolic stroke qualifies as cerebrovascular disease → 10. No malignancy, heart failure, or chronic renal disease → 0 for each.
- Examination: alert; RR 19 (<30/min), systolic BP 145 (≥90 mm Hg), temperature 36.9°C (neither <35 nor ≥40), and pulse 87 (<125/min) → 0 for each.
- Laboratory findings: BUN 31 mg/dL meets the ≥30 threshold → 20. Arterial pH 7.44 (not <7.35), sodium 137 (not <130 mEq/L), glucose 118 (not ≥250 mg/dL), and hematocrit 45% (not <30%) → 0 for each. Room-air PaO₂ 78 mm Hg and saturation 91% do not meet the <60 mm Hg or <90% oxygenation threshold → 0.
- Imaging: left pleural effusion → 10.
Total = 48 + 20 + 10 + 20 + 10 = 108.
Final answer: 108
